question.text: Under New Jersey law, who in a passenger vehicle must wear a seat belt?

answer.text: New Jersey law requires the driver and every passenger of a passenger vehicle, such as a car, van, pickup truck or SUV, to wear a seat belt.

teaching.text: The rule covers the driver and every passenger, so no seat in a car, van, pickup or SUV is a belt-free seat. Remember: Everyone aboard buckles up.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: New Jersey law requires the driver and every passenger of a passenger vehicle, such as a car, van, pickup truck or SUV, to wear a seat belt.

question.text: Why can a police officer stop a vehicle just because the driver, a front-seat passenger or a child is unbelted?

answer.text: An unbelted driver, front-seat passenger or child under eighteen is a primary offense, so a police officer may stop the vehicle for that violation alone.

teaching.text: Primary means the unbelted driver, front-seat passenger or child is reason enough for the stop on its own. Remember: Front unbelted means primary stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An unbelted driver, front-seat passenger or child under eighteen is a primary offense, so a police officer may stop the vehicle for that violation alone.

question.text: When can an unbuckled back-seat rider who is eighteen or older receive a seat belt summons?

answer.text: Unbuckled back-seat riders aged eighteen or older can receive a summons under a secondary law, but only when the vehicle has been stopped for some other reason.

teaching.text: Back-seat adults are still covered, but the summons only follows a stop made for some other reason. Remember: Adult back seat waits.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Unbuckled back-seat riders aged eighteen or older can receive a summons under a secondary law, but only when the vehicle has been stopped for some other reason.

question.text: What separates the primary seat belt offense from the secondary rule for adult back-seat riders?

answer.text: An unbelted driver, front-seat passenger or child under eighteen can be the only reason for a traffic stop, whereas an unbelted back-seat rider aged eighteen or older can be ticketed only after a stop for something else.

teaching.text: Ask two questions: which seat, and how old. Front seat or under eighteen means primary; a back-seat adult means secondary. Remember: Front alone stops, back waits.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An unbelted driver, front-seat passenger or child under eighteen can be the only reason for a traffic stop, whereas an unbelted back-seat rider aged eighteen or older can be ticketed only after a stop for something else.

question.text: Who is answerable for belting passengers under eighteen, and who answers for front-seat adults?

answer.text: The driver is answerable for every passenger under age eighteen, while front-seat passengers aged eighteen or older are answerable for themselves.

teaching.text: Age decides it: the driver answers for anyone under eighteen, and front-seat adults answer for their own belts. Remember: Driver owns the kids' belts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The driver is answerable for every passenger under age eighteen, while front-seat passengers aged eighteen or older are answerable for themselves.

question.text: What seat belt duty does a GDL permit or probationary license holder carry?

answer.text: A driver holding a GDL permit or probationary license must wear a seat belt and must also make every passenger, in any seat, buckle up.

teaching.text: A GDL driver's duty is wider than an ordinary driver's, covering every passenger of every age in every seat. Remember: GDL buckles every seat.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver holding a GDL permit or probationary license must wear a seat belt and must also make every passenger, in any seat, buckle up.

question.text: How does an ordinary driver's belt duty differ from a GDL holder's?

answer.text: An ordinary driver answers for belting passengers under eighteen, but a GDL permit or probationary license holder must make passengers of every age buckle up.

teaching.text: Ordinary drivers look after the minors, while GDL permit and probationary drivers look after everyone in the car. Remember: Ordinary minors, GDL everyone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An ordinary driver answers for belting passengers under eighteen, but a GDL permit or probationary license holder must make passengers of every age buckle up.

question.text: Which vehicles and people does the New Jersey seat belt law exempt?

answer.text: The seat belt law exempts passenger vehicles built before July one, nineteen sixty-six, vehicles that federal law does not require to have belts, and people with a physical or medical reason confirmed in writing by a licensed physician.

teaching.text: The exemptions are narrow: very old vehicles, vehicles federal law does not require to have belts, and a physician's written medical reason. Remember: Old cars, exempt vehicles, doctor's note.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The seat belt law exempts passenger vehicles built before July one, nineteen sixty-six, vehicles that federal law does not require to have belts, and people with a physical or medical reason confirmed in writing by a licensed physician.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Old cars, exempt vehicles, doctor's note

question.text: How must a driver secure a passenger who uses a wheelchair?

answer.text: A driver who carries a passenger using a wheelchair must secure that person with a correctly adjusted, fastened wheelchair and occupant securement device.

teaching.text: A wheelchair rider is secured with a proper securement device that is fastened and correctly adjusted. Remember: Wheelchair secured, fastened, adjusted.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver who carries a passenger using a wheelchair must secure that person with a correctly adjusted, fastened wheelchair and occupant securement device.

question.text: By how much does wearing a seat belt improve a motorist's chance of surviving a crash?

answer.text: Wearing a seat belt improves a motorist's chance of surviving a crash by sixty percent.

teaching.text: Sixty percent is the figure for the seat belt itself, so keep it separate from the shoulder strap figure. Remember: Belt adds sixty percent.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Wearing a seat belt improves a motorist's chance of surviving a crash by sixty percent.

question.text: How much better are crash survival odds with both a seat belt and a shoulder strap?

answer.text: Survival odds in a crash are three to four times better when a motorist wears both a seat belt and a shoulder strap.

teaching.text: Belt plus shoulder strap is the stronger combination, which is why its figure is a multiple rather than a percentage. Remember: Strap too, three to four times.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Survival odds in a crash are three to four times better when a motorist wears both a seat belt and a shoulder strap.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Strap too, three to four times

question.text: Hitting the dashboard or windshield at thirty miles per hour is compared with what?

answer.text: Hitting the dashboard or windshield at thirty miles per hour is compared with falling from the top of a three-story building.

teaching.text: Even a city speed like thirty miles per hour produces an impact the manual compares with a long, hard fall. Remember: Thirty equals a three-story fall.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hitting the dashboard or windshield at thirty miles per hour is compared with falling from the top of a three-story building.

question.text: About how long does buckling up take?

answer.text: Buckling up takes only about three seconds.

teaching.text: The cost of buckling up is tiny compared with the protection it gives on every trip. Remember: Three seconds to click.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Buckling up takes only about three seconds.

question.text: How do seat belts make crash injuries likely to be less severe?

answer.text: Belts slow the body down together with the vehicle and keep occupants from being thrown out in a crash, so injuries are likely to be less severe.

teaching.text: Belts work by keeping your body moving with the vehicle and keeping you inside it, which is why injuries tend to be less severe. Remember: Slow with the car, stay inside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Belts slow the body down together with the vehicle and keep occupants from being thrown out in a crash, so injuries are likely to be less severe.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Slow with the car, stay inside

question.text: Where should the lap belt and the shoulder belt sit on your body?

answer.text: The lap belt should sit under the abdomen and low on the hips, and the shoulder belt should cross the collarbone and breastbone while staying away from the neck.

teaching.text: Low on the hips and across the collarbone and breastbone is the goal, with the shoulder belt kept off the neck. Remember: Low on hips, off neck.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The lap belt should sit under the abdomen and low on the hips, and the shoulder belt should cross the collarbone and breastbone while staying away from the neck.

question.text: Is it safe to fasten one seat belt around two people?

answer.text: Never fasten one belt around two people.

teaching.text: Sharing a belt is never allowed, no matter how small the riders or how short the trip. Remember: One belt, one body.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never fasten one belt around two people.

question.text: If a car has air bags, when should you still wear both the lap and shoulder belts?

answer.text: Because air bags are only supplemental protection, both the lap and shoulder belts should be worn on every trip and in every seat, back seat included.

teaching.text: Air bags are an add-on, not a substitute, so both belts stay on in every seat, back seat included. Remember: Every trip, every seat.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Because air bags are only supplemental protection, both the lap and shoulder belts should be worn on every trip and in every seat, back seat included.

question.text: What must every child restraint system made since January one, one thousand nine hundred eighty-one, be designed to do, and what label does it carry?

answer.text: Every child restraint system made since January one, nineteen eighty-one, must be designed to pass demanding safety tests and carries a label giving its manufacture date and its conformity with federal safety standards.

teaching.text: Look for the label on the seat: it gives the manufacture date and shows the seat meets federal safety standards. Remember: Tested seats carry dated labels.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Every child restraint system made since January one, nineteen eighty-one, must be designed to pass demanding safety tests and carries a label giving its manufacture date and its conformity with federal safety standards.

question.text: Which way must an infant seat never face, and what does the seat label show?

answer.text: An infant seat must never be turned to face forward, and the seat label shows the child size and weight it is designed to protect.

teaching.text: An infant seat stays rear-facing, and its label tells you the size and weight of child it is built for. Remember: Infants never face forward.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An infant seat must never be turned to face forward, and the seat label shows the child size and weight it is designed to protect.

question.text: What is the best protection a driver can give a child in a car seat?

answer.text: Using the car seat on every ride and using it correctly each time, following the seat's own instructions, is the best protection a driver can give a child.

teaching.text: A good seat only protects when it is used on every ride and installed the way its own instructions say. Remember: Every ride, used right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Using the car seat on every ride and using it correctly each time, following the seat's own instructions, is the best protection a driver can give a child.

question.text: According to the manual, how must children under age two, and those under thirty pounds, ride?

answer.text: The manual says children under age two and those weighing under thirty pounds must ride in a rear-facing child restraint equipped with a five-point harness.

teaching.text: The youngest step is the only one that requires a rear-facing seat, always with a five-point harness. Remember: Under two faces the back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The manual says children under age two and those weighing under thirty pounds must ride in a rear-facing child restraint equipped with a five-point harness.

question.text: How must children under age four who weigh under forty pounds ride?

answer.text: Children under age four who weigh under forty pounds must ride in a rear seat in a five-point-harness restraint, either rear-facing until they outgrow the maker's limits and then forward-facing, or forward-facing.

teaching.text: The second step keeps the five-point harness and the rear seat, but allows forward-facing once the maker's limits are outgrown. Remember: Under four, harness, rear seat.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Children under age four who weigh under forty pounds must ride in a rear seat in a five-point-harness restraint, either rear-facing until they outgrow the maker's limits and then forward-facing, or forward-facing.

question.text: How must children under age eight who are shorter than fifty-seven inches ride?

answer.text: Children under age eight and shorter than fifty-seven inches (four feet, nine inches) must ride in a rear seat, either in a forward-facing restraint with a five-point harness until they outgrow it and then a booster seat, or in a booster seat.

teaching.text: The third step moves from harness to booster as the child grows, and the child still rides in a rear seat. Remember: Under eight, harness or booster.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Children under age eight and shorter than fifty-seven inches (four feet, nine inches) must ride in a rear seat, either in a forward-facing restraint with a five-point harness until they outgrow it and then a booster seat, or in a booster seat.

question.text: What are the three child-seat thresholds that are easy to mix up?

answer.text: Three child-seat thresholds are easy to mix up: under age two or under thirty pounds means rear-facing, under four and under forty pounds means a harness in a rear seat, and under eight and under fifty-seven inches means a harness or booster in a rear seat.

teaching.text: Pair each age with its own number: two with thirty pounds, four with forty pounds, eight with fifty-seven inches. Remember: Two, four, eight in steps.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Three child-seat thresholds are easy to mix up: under age two or under thirty pounds means rear-facing, under four and under forty pounds means a harness in a rear seat, and under eight and under fifty-seven inches means a harness or booster in a rear seat.

question.text: Where must all children under age eight sit, and when may they ride up front?

answer.text: All children under age eight must sit in a rear seat, and only a vehicle with no rear seat allows them to ride in an approved restraint or booster seat up front.

teaching.text: The rear seat is the rule for children under eight; the front is allowed only when the vehicle has no rear seat at all. Remember: Under eight in back unless none.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: All children under age eight must sit in a rear seat, and only a vehicle with no rear seat allows them to ride in an approved restraint or booster seat up front.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Under eight in back unless none

question.text: Which children may an autocycle operator not carry?

answer.text: An autocycle operator may not carry any child who would have to ride in a child passenger restraint under the child passenger safety law.

teaching.text: If a child would need a child passenger restraint, that child cannot ride on an autocycle. Remember: No restraint kids on autocycles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An autocycle operator may not carry any child who would have to ride in a child passenger restraint under the child passenger safety law.

question.text: What can a violation of the child passenger safety law cost?

answer.text: Violating the child passenger safety law can bring a fine of fifty dollars to seventy-five dollars, plus fees and court costs.

teaching.text: The fine is only part of the cost, since fees and court costs can be added on top. Remember: Fifty to seventy-five, plus costs.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Violating the child passenger safety law can bring a fine of fifty dollars to seventy-five dollars, plus fees and court costs.

question.text: What are air bags meant to do, and in which new vehicles do federal standards require them?

answer.text: Air bags are meant to add to seat belt protection in frontal crashes, and federal standards require them in all new passenger cars and light trucks.

teaching.text: Air bags support the belt in frontal crashes, and federal standards make them standard in new cars and light trucks. Remember: Air bags add to belts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Air bags are meant to add to seat belt protection in frontal crashes, and federal standards require them in all new passenger cars and light trucks.

question.text: How fast can air bags inflate, and when does a correctly belted average adult usually reach the bag?

answer.text: Air bags can inflate at speeds up to two hundred miles per hour, and a correctly belted adult of average size usually reaches the bag only after it is fully inflated.

teaching.text: The bag inflates with great speed, and a properly belted average adult usually meets it once it is already fully inflated. Remember: Two hundred, then fully inflated.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Air bags can inflate at speeds up to two hundred miles per hour, and a correctly belted adult of average size usually reaches the bag only after it is fully inflated.

question.text: Whom have air bags helped, and whom could they seriously hurt?

answer.text: Air bags have saved many belted adults but could seriously injure or kill children sitting in the front seat.

teaching.text: The same force that protects belted adults can seriously hurt a child sitting up front. Remember: Saves adults, endangers front kids.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Air bags have saved many belted adults but could seriously injure or kill children sitting in the front seat.

question.text: Where may a rear-facing child restraint never be placed?

answer.text: A rear-facing child restraint may never be placed in a front seat that has a passenger-side air bag that has not been disabled or turned off.

teaching.text: A rear-facing seat and an active passenger air bag must never share the front seat. Remember: Rear-facing never meets live bag.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A rear-facing child restraint may never be placed in a front seat that has a passenger-side air bag that has not been disabled or turned off.

question.text: Children of what age should always ride in the back seat?

answer.text: Children twelve years old and younger should always ride in the back seat.

teaching.text: Twelve and under means the back seat, every trip, which keeps children away from front air bags. Remember: Twelve and under ride back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Children twelve years old and younger should always ride in the back seat.

question.text: Where and how should an infant ride in a vehicle that has air bags?

answer.text: An infant should always ride in a rear-facing infant safety seat in the back seat of a vehicle that has air bags.

teaching.text: The default for an infant in a car with air bags is simple: rear-facing seat, back seat. Remember: Infant rear-facing, back seat.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An infant should always ride in a rear-facing infant safety seat in the back seat of a vehicle that has air bags.

question.text: How can you tell that a vehicle has an air bag?

answer.text: A vehicle has an air bag when the steering wheel and dashboard panel show the words air bag or the letters SRS or SIR.

teaching.text: The words air bag, or the letters SRS or SIR, on the wheel or dash tell you the vehicle has one. Remember: Look for SRS or SIR.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A vehicle has an air bag when the steering wheel and dashboard panel show the words air bag or the letters SRS or SIR.

question.text: Besides the steering wheel and dashboard, where may makers place air bag warning labels?

answer.text: Besides the steering wheel and dashboard markings, makers may place air bag warning labels on the sun visors, on the sides of the open-door frame, or in the owner's manual.

teaching.text: Warning labels can also appear on the sun visors, the edges of the open-door frame, or in the owner's manual. Remember: Visors, door frame, manual.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Besides the steering wheel and dashboard markings, makers may place air bag warning labels on the sun visors, on the sides of the open-door frame, or in the owner's manual.

question.text: What did NHTSA allow in one thousand nine hundred ninety-five, and what did it allow from January one thousand nine hundred ninety-eight?

answer.text: In nineteen ninety-five NHTSA allowed air bag cutoff switches in pickup trucks, sports cars and cars with no back seat, and from January nineteen ninety-eight it let repair shops and dealers install switches after an approved application.

teaching.text: NHTSA first allowed cutoff switches in a few vehicle types, then later let shops and dealers install them after an approved application. Remember: Limited switches, then shop installs.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In nineteen ninety-five NHTSA allowed air bag cutoff switches in pickup trucks, sports cars and cars with no back seat, and from January nineteen ninety-eight it let repair shops and dealers install switches after an approved application.

question.text: Who is a switch for both the driver and passenger air bags meant for?

answer.text: A switch for both driver and passenger air bags is for people whose medical condition makes a deploying air bag riskier than hitting the wheel, dashboard or windshield.

teaching.text: A switch for both bags is about a medical condition that makes a deploying bag the bigger danger. Remember: Medical risk, both switched.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A switch for both driver and passenger air bags is for people whose medical condition makes a deploying air bag riskier than hitting the wheel, dashboard or windshield.

question.text: Who is a driver-side air bag switch for, and who is a passenger-side switch for?

answer.text: A driver-side air bag switch is for drivers who cannot keep at least ten inches between the steering wheel center and the breastbone center, while a passenger-side switch is for drivers who must seat an infant, or a child aged one to twelve, in front.

teaching.text: Match the switch to the reason: sitting too close points to the driver side, seating a child up front points to the passenger side. Remember: Driver ten inches, passenger child.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver-side air bag switch is for drivers who cannot keep at least ten inches between the steering wheel center and the breastbone center, while a passenger-side switch is for drivers who must seat an infant, or a child aged one to twelve, in front.

question.text: When should backup lights come on, and when does New Jersey law forbid them?

answer.text: Backup lights should come on when reversing, and New Jersey law forbids having any backup light on while the vehicle is moving forward.

teaching.text: Backup lights belong to reversing only; showing one while moving forward breaks New Jersey law. Remember: Backup lights only backing up.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Backup lights should come on when reversing, and New Jersey law forbids having any backup light on while the vehicle is moving forward.

question.text: How should you check your brake lights, and why replace broken light covers?

answer.text: Get a helper to check the brake lights, and replace broken light covers because their glare can affect the driver behind.

teaching.text: You cannot see your own brake lights from the seat, so a helper does the checking, and broken covers get replaced. Remember: Helper checks, covers replaced.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Get a helper to check the brake lights, and replace broken light covers because their glare can affect the driver behind.

question.text: What must be true of your high and low beams, and what may drivers flashing at your low beams mean?

answer.text: High and low beams must both work and be aimed correctly; other drivers flashing their lights at your low beams may mean your headlights are out of line.

teaching.text: Both beams need to work and be aimed right, and flashing from other drivers can be the first hint that they are not. Remember: Flashed at? Check your aim.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: High and low beams must both work and be aimed correctly; other drivers flashing their lights at your low beams may mean your headlights are out of line.

question.text: Which signs mean your brakes need checking?

answer.text: Brakes need checking if the vehicle pulls to one side when stopping, the pedal feels taut, or there is unusual squealing or grinding.

teaching.text: Pulling, a taut pedal, or squealing and grinding are each a reason to have the brakes checked. Remember: Pulls, taut pedal, grinding.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Brakes need checking if the vehicle pulls to one side when stopping, the pedal feels taut, or there is unusual squealing or grinding.

question.text: What should you do with conventional disc and drum brakes after driving through water, and why?

answer.text: After driving through water, gently pump conventional disc and drum brakes to test and dry them, since braking hard could lock them up.

teaching.text: Water calls for gentle pumping on conventional brakes, because a hard stop could lock them up. Remember: Wet brakes, pump gently.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After driving through water, gently pump conventional disc and drum brakes to test and dry them, since braking hard could lock them up.

question.text: How are anti-lock brakes tested, and what should you never do with them while braking?

answer.text: Anti-lock brakes are tested with steady pressure on the pedal, and a driver should never pump ABS brakes or jerk the steering wheel while braking.

teaching.text: Anti-lock brakes want steady pressure, with no pumping and no jerking of the wheel. Remember: ABS steady, never pumped.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Anti-lock brakes are tested with steady pressure on the pedal, and a driver should never pump ABS brakes or jerk the steering wheel while braking.

question.text: How does handling conventional brakes after water differ from handling anti-lock brakes?

answer.text: Conventional disc and drum brakes are pumped gently after driving through water, while anti-lock brakes are pressed steadily and never pumped.

teaching.text: The two brake types are handled in opposite ways: conventional brakes are pumped gently after water, anti-lock brakes are pressed steadily. Remember: Pump drums, press ABS.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Conventional disc and drum brakes are pumped gently after driving through water, while anti-lock brakes are pressed steadily and never pumped.

question.text: On what kind of surface may anti-lock brakes make the stopping distance longer?

answer.text: On very soft surfaces such as loose gravel or unpacked snow, anti-lock brakes may make the stopping distance longer.

teaching.text: Anti-lock brakes do not always shorten a stop; on loose gravel or unpacked snow the distance may grow. Remember: Soft ground, longer ABS stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On very soft surfaces such as loose gravel or unpacked snow, anti-lock brakes may make the stopping distance longer.

question.text: Within what distance should a vehicle stop from twenty miles per hour, and how can you test it?

answer.text: A vehicle should be able to stop within twenty-five feet from twenty miles per hour, which a driver can test in an empty parking lot using chalk marks.

teaching.text: Twenty miles per hour should stop within twenty-five feet, and chalk marks in an empty lot let you check it. Remember: Twenty stops in twenty-five feet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A vehicle should be able to stop within twenty-five feet from twenty miles per hour, which a driver can test in an empty parking lot using chalk marks.

question.text: When should you sound your horn, and how often?

answer.text: Sound the horn to signal that you are passing, to announce yourself as you leave a blind alley, curve or driveway, or to warn another driver of danger, but do not overuse it.

teaching.text: The horn is for passing, for announcing yourself where others cannot see you, and for warning of danger, never for overuse. Remember: Pass, emerge, warn, never overuse.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Sound the horn to signal that you are passing, to announce yourself as you leave a blind alley, curve or driveway, or to warn another driver of danger, but do not overuse it.

question.text: On a straight, level road, how should a sound vehicle steer?

answer.text: On a straight, level road the vehicle should keep a straight course with no front-end shimmy and without excess play in the steering wheel.

teaching.text: On a straight, level road a healthy vehicle tracks straight, without front-end shimmy or a loose steering wheel. Remember: Straight, no shimmy, no play.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a straight, level road the vehicle should keep a straight course with no front-end shimmy and without excess play in the steering wheel.

question.text: What should you do when your turn signals fail?

answer.text: When the turn signals fail, repair them quickly and give hand signals until they work again.

teaching.text: Hand signals fill the gap while failed turn signals are being repaired. Remember: Signals out, hands out.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When the turn signals fail, repair them quickly and give hand signals until they work again.

question.text: When should you check tire pressure, and where do you find the right pressure?

answer.text: Check tire pressure often, especially while the tires are cold, using the pressure listed in the owner's manual or on the driver's door jamb.

teaching.text: Check pressure often, especially when the tires are cold, and take the right number from the owner's manual or the door jamb. Remember: Check cold, match the jamb.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Check tire pressure often, especially while the tires are cold, using the pressure listed in the owner's manual or on the driver's door jamb.

question.text: How worn is too worn for tire tread, and which tires should not be mixed?

answer.text: Do not drive on tires with less than one sixteenth inch of tread, roughly the edge of a penny, and do not mix radials with other tire types.

teaching.text: Tread worn to about the edge of a penny is too thin to drive on, and radials should not be mixed with other types. Remember: Penny edge, no mixing radials.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not drive on tires with less than one sixteenth inch of tread, roughly the edge of a penny, and do not mix radials with other tire types.

question.text: Where does New Jersey prohibit add-on window tinting?

answer.text: New Jersey prohibits add-on tinting on the windshield and the front side windows.

teaching.text: Add-on tint is kept off the windshield and the front side windows. Remember: No tint up front.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: New Jersey prohibits add-on tinting on the windshield and the front side windows.

question.text: What must a motorist try to do about built-up snow and ice before driving?

answer.text: Before driving, a motorist must make every reasonable effort to clear built-up snow and ice from the exposed surfaces of the vehicle, including the hood, trunk, roof and windshield.

teaching.text: Clearing snow means the whole vehicle, roof, hood and trunk included, not just a hole in the windshield. Remember: Clear the roof too.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before driving, a motorist must make every reasonable effort to clear built-up snow and ice from the exposed surfaces of the vehicle, including the hood, trunk, roof and windshield.

question.text: What fines apply for not clearing snow or ice from a vehicle?

answer.text: Not clearing snow or ice brings a fine of twenty-five dollars to seventy-five dollars even if none falls off, and fines up to one thousand five hundred dollars when falling snow or ice causes injury or property damage.

teaching.text: There are two levels: a smaller fine even when nothing falls, and a much larger one when falling snow or ice causes harm. Remember: Small fine always, big if harm.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Not clearing snow or ice brings a fine of twenty-five dollars to seventy-five dollars even if none falls off, and fines up to one thousand five hundred dollars when falling snow or ice causes injury or property damage.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Small fine always, big if harm

question.text: Does the snow and ice fine apply if nothing comes loose from the vehicle?

answer.text: The snow and ice fine applies whether or not any snow or ice actually comes loose from the vehicle.

teaching.text: The fine is for failing to clear the vehicle, so it applies even if nothing comes loose. Remember: No falling chunk needed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The snow and ice fine applies whether or not any snow or ice actually comes loose from the vehicle.

question.text: What is carbon monoxide, and where can it build up?

answer.text: Carbon monoxide is an odorless, colorless gas in vehicle exhaust that can build up to deadly levels in or around a vehicle.

teaching.text: You cannot see or smell carbon monoxide, which is what makes a build-up so dangerous. Remember: Invisible, odorless exhaust danger.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Carbon monoxide is an odorless, colorless gas in vehicle exhaust that can build up to deadly levels in or around a vehicle.

question.text: Which vehicle faults and driving conditions can let carbon monoxide build up?

answer.text: Driving with an exhaust leak or a poorly tuned engine, or with the trunk or rear tailgate open, can let carbon monoxide build up.

teaching.text: Exhaust leaks, a poorly tuned engine, or an open trunk or tailgate can all let the gas build up. Remember: Leaks, bad tune, open tailgate.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving with an exhaust leak or a poorly tuned engine, or with the trunk or rear tailgate open, can let carbon monoxide build up.

question.text: Besides exhaust leaks, what else can let carbon monoxide build up?

answer.text: Carbon monoxide can also build up from holes in the vehicle body, from a tailpipe blocked by snow, leaves or water, and from idling in a garage or other enclosed space even with the outside door open.

teaching.text: An open garage door does not make idling inside safe, and blocked tailpipes or body holes can also let the gas build up. Remember: Open garage door still deadly.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Carbon monoxide can also build up from holes in the vehicle body, from a tailpipe blocked by snow, leaves or water, and from idling in a garage or other enclosed space even with the outside door open.

question.text: Why can't you count on symptoms to warn you about carbon monoxide?

answer.text: Carbon monoxide can kill before a person notices any symptom such as headache, dizziness, nausea, chest pain, confusion or loss of consciousness.

teaching.text: Symptoms can come too late, so suspicion alone is reason enough to act. Remember: Kills before you notice.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Carbon monoxide can kill before a person notices any symptom such as headache, dizziness, nausea, chest pain, confusion or loss of consciousness.

question.text: What should you do if you suspect carbon monoxide poisoning?

answer.text: If carbon monoxide poisoning is suspected, move the person away from the source and call nine one one; in a vehicle, switch off the engine and get out as soon as it is safe.

teaching.text: Get the person away from the source and call for emergency help; in a vehicle, switch off the engine and get out once it is safe. Remember: Away, call, engine off, out.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If carbon monoxide poisoning is suspected, move the person away from the source and call nine one one; in a vehicle, switch off the engine and get out as soon as it is safe.

question.text: Before getting into the vehicle, where should you look, and why?

answer.text: Before getting into the vehicle, look both in front of it and behind it, because children or objects may be hidden in spots the driver cannot see from the seat.

teaching.text: Hidden children or objects can sit where the driver's seat gives no view, so look in front and behind before getting in. Remember: Front and back first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before getting into the vehicle, look both in front of it and behind it, because children or objects may be hidden in spots the driver cannot see from the seat.

question.text: What should be set and checked before you move off?

answer.text: Before moving off, the seat should let you reach every pedal and control (about an arm's length from the wheel for most drivers), the mirrors should be adjusted, belts fastened, the gear in park or neutral with the parking brake set, and the doors locked.

teaching.text: Setup comes before moving: seat within reach of every control, mirrors, belts, park or neutral with the brake set, doors locked. Remember: Seat, mirrors, belts, park, locks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before moving off, the seat should let you reach every pedal and control (about an arm's length from the wheel for most drivers), the mirrors should be adjusted, belts fastened, the gear in park or neutral with the parking brake set, and the doors locked.

question.text: How much of the information a driver needs comes through vision?

answer.text: More than ninety-five percent of the information a driver needs comes through vision.

teaching.text: Nearly all the information you use while driving comes through your eyes. Remember: Driving is mostly seeing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: More than ninety-five percent of the information a driver needs comes through vision.

question.text: How often should a motorist have an eye examination?

answer.text: A motorist should have an eye examination every two years.

teaching.text: Regular eye exams keep your most important driving sense in check. Remember: Eyes checked every two years.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A motorist should have an eye examination every two years.

question.text: What should you skip, and what should you choose, to cut night glare?

answer.text: To cut night glare, skip colored lenses because they distort color, and choose anti-reflective lens coatings.

teaching.text: Colored lenses distort color, so anti-reflective coatings are the better choice against night glare. Remember: Skip tints, choose anti-reflective.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To cut night glare, skip colored lenses because they distort color, and choose anti-reflective lens coatings.

question.text: How does age change vision, according to the manual's example?

answer.text: With age, visual clarity and side vision fade; in the manual's example, a person of sixty takes in only about one third of the light that a person of twenty does.

teaching.text: Aging eyes take in far less light, along with fading clarity and side vision. Remember: Sixty sees a third.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With age, visual clarity and side vision fade; in the manual's example, a person of sixty takes in only about one third of the light that a person of twenty does.

question.text: How should the outside mirror be set?

answer.text: Set the outside mirror so the tip of the driver-side front door handle appears in the lower right of the mirror.

teaching.text: The tip of the door handle in the lower right corner is your reference point for the outside mirror. Remember: Door handle tip, lower right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Set the outside mirror so the tip of the driver-side front door handle appears in the lower right of the mirror.

question.text: How can you check your mirrors on the road using a passing car?

answer.text: To check the mirrors on the road, let a car pass on the left: as it leaves the inside mirror, its front bumper should already show in the outside mirror.

teaching.text: A passing car should hand off smoothly from the inside mirror to the outside mirror. Remember: Leaves inside, bumper outside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To check the mirrors on the road, let a car pass on the left: as it leaves the inside mirror, its front bumper should already show in the outside mirror.

question.text: After starting the engine, how should you confirm the path is clear?

answer.text: After starting the engine, turn and look back to confirm the path is clear rather than relying on the rearview mirrors, and watch for pedestrians, bicycles and mopeds.

teaching.text: Mirrors alone are not enough; turning to look back confirms the path and catches pedestrians, bicycles and mopeds. Remember: Turn your head, not mirrors.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After starting the engine, turn and look back to confirm the path is clear rather than relying on the rearview mirrors, and watch for pedestrians, bicycles and mopeds.

question.text: What idling limit does New Jersey require of every motorist?

answer.text: New Jersey requires every motorist to keep vehicle idling to three minutes or less.

teaching.text: The idling limit applies to every motorist and is measured in minutes, not hours. Remember: Three minutes, no more.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: New Jersey requires every motorist to keep vehicle idling to three minutes or less.

question.text: Does the three-minute idling limit apply in every situation?

answer.text: Some situations allow longer idling, such as sitting in traffic or waiting at a drive-thru, so the three-minute limit has listed exemptions.

teaching.text: The limit has listed exemptions, such as sitting in traffic or waiting at a drive-thru. Remember: Traffic and drive-thru excepted.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Some situations allow longer idling, such as sitting in traffic or waiting at a drive-thru, so the three-minute limit has listed exemptions.

question.text: What fines do vehicle and property owners face for each idling violation?

answer.text: Vehicle and property owners face fines of two hundred fifty dollars to one thousand dollars for each idling violation.

teaching.text: The fines fall on vehicle and property owners and apply to each violation separately. Remember: Two fifty to a thousand.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Vehicle and property owners face fines of two hundred fifty dollars to one thousand dollars for each idling violation.

hooks_spoken: The driver and every passenger buckle up; an unbelted driver, front-seat rider or child is enough for a stop, while adult back-seat riders are ticketed only after a stop for something else.

Exemptions cover very old vehicles, vehicles that federal law does not require to have belts, and a doctor's written reason.

hooks_spoken: A belt adds sixty percent to your survival chance, and a belt with a shoulder strap makes the odds three to four times better.
Lap belt low on the hips, shoulder belt across the collarbone and away from the neck, one belt per person, in every seat.

hooks_spoken: Under two or under thirty pounds rides rear-facing; under four and under forty pounds stays in a harness in back; under eight and under fifty-seven inches uses a harness or booster in back.
Children under eight sit in back unless the vehicle has no rear seat, and an infant seat never faces forward.

hooks_spoken: Air bags add to belts but can seriously hurt children up front, so children twelve and younger ride in back and a rear-facing seat never sits before an active passenger air bag.
Look for the words air bag or the letters SRS or SIR on the wheel and dash.
A driver-side switch fits drivers who cannot keep ten inches from the wheel, and a passenger-side switch fits drivers who must seat a child in front.

hooks_spoken: Pump conventional brakes gently after water, but press anti-lock brakes steadily and never pump them.
A sound vehicle stops within twenty-five feet from twenty miles per hour, though anti-lock brakes may stop longer on loose gravel or unpacked snow.
Backup lights belong to reversing only.
